results.evidence: The route page for the North Buttress Couloir says it is usually in condition as soon as the trailhead opens; a regional outdoors guide treats it as a winter/spring snow climb timed around the frozen lake (ice breaking up about mid-May); peak route summaries say it is most often climbed in winter or early spring while the couloir is fully filled with snow, with Class 4 rock showing later in summer. None describes a September-October window. The row's own best_season, approach_variants season (Mar-Jun) and climate.fall already agree; `season` is the outlier and also broke the short-window format.

patches.expect: Best in a cool, stable freeze — commonly climbed late April-May or Sep-Oct

results.evidence: The route page grades the Northeast Buttress 5.8+, Grade IV, 14 pitches, and describes the crux pitches 9-10 as gaining a left-facing corner to the ridge crest at 5.8-5.9. A separate route write-up describes sustained 5.8 climbing. No source grades the route or its crux a clean 5.9, so the headline 5.8+ stands and the two cells that print a bare 5.9 for the crux are brought to 5.8-5.9 (matching beta and the climbing_route prose).

results.correct_value: watch_out describing this summer rock route with its walk-off glacier descent
results.evidence: The route page describes a 14-pitch 5.8+ rock route with a walk-off descent down the Colchuck Glacier, and a June 2018 ascent report describes a dry rock climb with a descent on dirt, rock and snow to the col and down the glacier, with no rappels and no ice or mixed pitches. The stored watch_out (M4 mixed, an ice bulge on pitch 3, a corniced rappel descent, 'near Snoqualmie Pass') belongs to a different winter route; it is replaced with warnings drawn from this row's own hazards, approach and descent.

patches.expect:
Highly conditions-dependent difficulty; mixed climbing (M4) pitches vary from easy snow/ice to sustained steep sections based on current conditions
Steep ice bulge (A2-3 rating) on pitch 3 with notoriously difficult anchor placement; anchors unreliable and sparingly available above pitch 3
Heavily corniced rappel descent; cornice collapse risk during warm spells; potential for rappel line being cut by cornices
S-shaped gully on pitch 1 with variable mixed climbing up to M4; conditions-dependent route difficulty affects protection options
Long pitch to base of ice bulge (70-80m) on easy terrain, but terrain becomes avalanche-prone on wider snow slopes
Exposed approach traverse; wind-loaded terrain near Snoqualmie Pass; rapid weather changes common
Multiple rappel anchors required for descent; deteriorating conditions during descent can create urgent retreat scenarios
patches.value:
Routefinding decides the day: the upper crux corner is easy to miss, and it is the most common reason parties retreat
Loose and mossy rock in places, especially the dirty chimney into the main dihedral and debris on the long ledge traverse
The moat at the foot of the buttress can be the hardest move of the approach in a lean snow year
A very long car-to-car day; expect to descend the Colchuck Glacier late, often by headlamp and on icy snow late in the season

results.correct_value: The approach does travel on the Colchuck Glacier, which holds few crevasses; the entry moat is the main gap
results.evidence: The route page says the Northeast Couloir is accessed from the Colchuck Glacier, higher up it than the North Buttress Couloir, and a winter ascent report describes travelling on the glacier to reach it. Two independent Colchuck Peak guides describe the Colchuck Glacier as a rapidly receding glacier with few if any crevasses that most parties cross unroped. So 'no glacier travel' is wrong, and the watch_out line's demand to always travel roped overstates it.

results.fact: Whether winter is the season's technical norm
results.correct_value: Winter through early spring in a stable, consolidated spell; late May-early June is the later window some parties use
results.evidence: A peak route summary says the Northeast Couloir is best done only under winter/early spring conditions; a February 2016 ascent report and a regional outdoors guide both describe it as a late-winter climb done in a stable spell on a consolidated snowpack (skiing across the frozen lake before its ice breaks up around mid-May). The first ascent was January 1975. The row's season text and itinerary.cal (Feb-May) agree; seasonal_guidance's optimal window and April note, which treat winter conditions as a reason not to go, are the outliers. Only the window and April's reason are changed; month statuses are left as stored.

results.fact: Summit-day length and start time: partner_requirements vs timing/itinerary
results.evidence: partner_requirements says an 8.5-hr round trip from a 04:00 start at camp, while timing and itinerary day 2 say a 2:30 AM start and an 11-hr summit push (back at camp 1:00 PM). The one ascent report found was a car-to-car ski day of roughly 10.75 hr from a 5:15 AM start, which settles neither camp-based figure; no second source gives a camp-to-camp time.

results.fact: Whether roping up for glacier travel is standard practice
results.correct_value: Rope is conditions-dependent: most parties go unroped on the bridged early-season glacier; rope up once crevasses or moats open
results.evidence: One Colchuck Peak guide says most people choose not to rope up on this glacier, which has shrunk and shows few if any crevasses; a second independent guide says it is a rapidly receding glacier with few crevasses so most parties do not rope, while advising parties to consider it at the toe. A guide service does rope its clients to the col, so roping is a choice, not a rule. gear, the waypoint directions and the approach text already say this; pro_tips' unconditional instruction is the outlier.

patches.expect: Rope up for glacier travel even when bridges look solid.
patches.value: Decide on the rope at the glacier's toe: many parties go unroped on the bridged early-season snow, but rope up once crevasses or moats have opened.
patches.fact: Whether roping up for glacier travel is standard practice

results.fact: Total elevation gain understates the trailhead-to-summit climb
results.evidence: Two independent Colchuck Peak guides give the car-to-car gain as about 5,300 ft (12.5 mi) and about 5,460 ft (12.6 mi); the row's own trailhead (3,400 ft) and summit (8,705 ft) give 5,305 ft, the figure the sibling Colchuck Glacier and Northeast Buttress rows use for the same climb. 2,800 ft is roughly the lake-to-summit gain only.
